newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST -- U.S. industrial sector throttles down.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST -- U.S. industrial sector throttles down.

text.p: U.S. manufacturers will likely cut production this winter, which should ease inflationary fears among Federal Reserve policy-makers, economists said.
Slower industrial output growth should coincide with flat or declining real gross domestic product (GDP) growth over the next several months, limiting price pressures, analysts said.

"The whole economy is ratcheting to a lower level of operation. Manufacturing certainly isn't going to be going like gangbusters under that scenario," said Ray Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards in St. Louis.
Number-crunchers will get a fresh peek inside the nation's factories when the Federal Reserve releases October industrial production and capacity utilization data on Friday at 0915 ET.
The consensus forecast of analysts polled by Reuters is for flat production, with capacity usage at U.S. factories, mines and utilities dipping to 83.0 percent from 83.3 percent in September.
Analysts pointed to the National Association of Purchasing Management's October report, which put its manufacturing activity index at 50.2, barely above neutral.
"That indicates we should get a dead-in-the-water reading for industrial production," said Kenneth Mayland, chief economist at Society National Bank.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and his fellow inflation-fighters should breathe a sigh of relief on any news of slowing industrial growth, which would likely help the central bank refrain from raising interest rates for several months, analysts said.
"That definitely helps the Fed," Worseck said. "In terms of growth, all sectors of the economy will be growing at lower rates in the next year."
Yet few economists are ready to predict a recession could follow a slowdown in the factory sector.
On the contrary, after annualized growth of near six percent in the second quarter and four percent in the third, the manufacturing sector could stand a healthy slowdown, said Mayland.
"Those numbers aren't sustainable in the long run without inflation pressures," Mayland said.
Real GDP growth could dip to as low as one percent annualized over the next two quarters, but should rebound somewhat later in 1997, analysts said.

"Is this current slowdown a prelude to a turndown? I don't think this is anything other than a down cycle within the overall cycle. We have not fully evolved the requisite preconditions for a turndown," Mayland said.
